preferences.free_language_preferences:
I want a traditional, unified campus where it's easy to make friends, 
                    rather than commuting in a massive, overwhelming city.

                    I'd love a place with cool museums, historical sites, good nightlife, 
                    and winters that aren't completely freezing.

                    Financially, I need an affordable city where rent and groceries won't 
                    drain my savings. My absolute max budget is $9,000 for the semester.

analysis.general_fit_reasoning: Small engineering school in a compact city with campus-style student life—good for making friends. Strasbourg offers strong historic museums and a lively but not overwhelming nightlife; winters are cool but not extreme. Relatively affordable compared with Paris and has an accessible Jewish community.

academic.grading_system_summary: Numeric scale from 0 to 20; minimum passing grade is 10 for exchange students to transfer credits.
academic.academic_summary_notes: Regular courseload is 30 ECTS/semester. Minimum for exchange students is 20 ECTS/semester for full-year stays (15 ECTS/semester allowed for 2nd-year students). Course selection for exchange programmes is done at time of application; double degree selection occurs at the start of each teaching period and 3rd-year/double-degree students must follow the full curriculum.

housing_and_logistics.housing_details: Limited on-campus housing available; application opens after official admission. Residences: Paris-Saclay Césal (€400–€750/month), Rennes Residence Belle Fontaine (€350–€450/month), Metz Residence Edouard Branly (€350–€450/month).
housing_and_logistics.medical_and_insurance_details: Health care insurance is mandatory. EU students: EHIC accepted. Non-EU students can take out French Social Security insurance upon arrival (free of charge; application link provided during registration). Upon arrival comprehensive coverage for lodging, personal liability and belongings is required.
housing_and_logistics.estimated_living_cost_per_month: Estimated budget for a full-year mobility is at least €700/month (including accommodation, food, internet); cost of living may be lower in Rennes and Metz.
housing_and_logistics.logistics_summary_notes: Non-EU students generally need to apply for a French visa and obtain a residence permit; incoming students are responsible for securing and paying for their visas. Health insurance is mandatory and details/registration are provided upon finalizing enrollment.

student_integration.language_course_details: Intensive French classes recommended/available at Cavilam - Alliance Française in Vichy prior to semester start. Admitted double-degree students are invited to a pre-program summer school focused on French language (costs not specified).
student_integration.integration_summary_notes: Orientation sessions/welcome events are organized (late August for fall/full year; late January for spring) and a Welcome Desk via Université Paris-Saclay provides arrival support; double-degree students have a preparatory summer school including French language.

analysis.general_fit_reasoning: Nicosia’s campus is compact and easier for forming social ties than a megacity commute. Good historical sites, museums and mild Mediterranean winters; nightlife is moderate and the international/erasmus crowd is smaller. Jewish/Israeli infrastructure is limited on the island.

academic.academic_summary_notes: A full-time semester workload is 30 ECTS. Course selection and detailed requirements are available via DTU's incoming exchange course information and course catalogue.

housing_and_logistics.housing_details: Accommodation information is provided via bdtu.dk and DTU's incoming exchange webpages; application procedures and deadlines are on the DTU exchange application pages.

student_integration.integration_summary_notes: An introduction week is offered and participants are appointed a buddy; additional student clubs and associations are available to support integration.

academic.academic_summary_notes: Full-time study equals 30 ECTS per semester (60 ECTS per academic year). No minimum number of credits is required, though some programmes (e.g., Design) specify minimums for participation (Design: min 6, max 30). Students may pick courses at both Bachelor and Master levels if prerequisites are met and the school approves; students are required to choose the majority of credits from their enrolled programme.

academic.instruction_languages: Most courses are in German; a number of courses are available in English (mainly at graduate level).

housing_and_logistics.estimated_living_cost_per_month: Housing €350-650 / food €150 / books & supplies €40 / health insurance (if not waived) €100; public transport approx. €180 per semester. Students applying for a visa/residence permit must demonstrate ~€934/month.
housing_and_logistics.logistics_summary_notes: Students needing a visa must prove sufficient funds (~€934/month). Housing via university is limited and not guaranteed; apply when instructed after exchange deadlines. Insurance is required unless waived and estimated at ~€100/month.

student_integration.language_course_details: Preparatory German intensive course offered early September/early March for approx. €295 (6 ECTS). Erasmus students eligible only with completed A2 German. German courses also available during the semester via ZEMS.
student_integration.integration_summary_notes: TU Berlin offers a preparatory German course and orientation sessions for exchange students and runs a buddy program to support integration.

academic.grading_system_summary: Local numeric scale 0-20 (French system); pass >=10 with subgroups A (outstanding) to E; FX/F for failures. ECTS maps passing students to A (top 10%), B (next 25%), C (next 30%), D (next 25%), E (last 10%); failures split into FX (local >=7) and F (local <7).
academic.academic_summary_notes: Courses are mainly taught in French (recommended CEFR level B1). Exchange students apply via the online portal and must meet nomination deadlines (1 Dec for autumn, 1 May for spring).

housing_and_logistics.housing_details: The institution provides guidance and assistance in finding accommodation and lists platforms such as HousingAnywhere and ESN; contact Incoming Relations Officer (incoming@centrale-marseille.fr) and international student webpages for support.

housing_and_logistics.logistics_summary_notes: The university assists with visa procedures and housing searches and provides insurance assistance; nomination deadlines are 1 Dec (autumn) and 1 May (spring), decisions sent within ~4 weeks and transcripts within ~5 weeks.

student_integration.integration_summary_notes: The International Students' Association (ICM) offers information and guidance to incoming students; institutional contacts (incoming@centrale-marseille.fr) and partner platforms (ESN) support integration and accommodation.

universities_fit_text: Small engineering school in a compact city with campus-style student life—good for making friends. Strasbourg offers strong historic museums and a lively but not overwhelming nightlife; winters are cool but not extreme. Relatively affordable compared with Paris and has an accessible Jewish community.

Nicosia’s campus is compact and easier for forming social ties than a megacity commute. Good historical sites, museums and mild Mediterranean winters; nightlife is moderate and the international/erasmus crowd is smaller. Jewish/Israeli infrastructure is limited on the island.

DTU is a suburban, highly residential campus with legendary campus bars and a strong peer network—excellent for easy social integration. Copenhagen offers world-class museums and nightlife; winters are chilly. Costs in Denmark are high, and there is a modest local Jewish community with some Chabad presence.

Located in a large Mediterranean port—campus life is mixed and less of a single enclosed bubble but still manageable. Excellent museums, historic port, vibrant nightlife and very mild winters. Generally more affordable than Paris and Marseille has an established Jewish community.

Elite, enclosed campus (Paris-Saclay) that functions like a unified residential bubble—very strong fit for wanting easy friend-making. Close enough to Paris for world-class museums and nightlife while maintaining a campus routine. Paris-area access gives excellent Jewish/Israeli community resources but overall living costs are high.

Small, campus-oriented applied-sciences university in a smaller city—strongly fits the unified-campus, easy-to-make-friends preference. Dessau has niche cultural assets (Bauhaus heritage) and close nature access but limited nightlife and a very small Jewish community. Cost of living is attractively low.

Hannover is a medium-sized city with a distributed campus footprint—okay but not ideal for a single unified campus experience. Decent local museums and moderate nightlife; winters are colder than Mediterranean options. Affordable compared with Germany’s largest cities and has a modest Jewish community.

Erlangen offers a compact student town atmosphere with good campus social life and easy friend-making; Nuremberg adds historic sites and museums. Solid student nightlife and reasonably affordable living. Jewish community presence exists but is smaller than in major capitals.

Top-tier research university—excellent academic fit. Munich is culturally rich with museums and nightlife but campuses are spread across the city rather than a single unified bubble, and living costs are high. Strong Jewish community and access to cultural institutions are a plus.

Classic small university town with a cohesive campus and easy social integration—very well aligned with the user's desire for a unified campus. Good access to nature (Thuringian Forest) and cultural history; winters are colder but manageable. Limited Jewish community presence locally.

Strong technical school with huge Erasmus and nightlife—very social but campuses are dispersed within a large city, so it clashes with the student's preference for a single, unified campus. Milan offers outstanding museums and historical sites and mild winters; Jewish community is active and accessible.

Iasi is a strong student city with a centralized campus feel and a lively local student scene—excellent for making friends quickly. Rich in history and churches with reasonable cultural life; winters can be chilly. Very affordable financially but has a very small Jewish community.

ORT in Montevideo provides a campus experience within a medium-sized city with a friendly student atmosphere. Montevideo offers cultural venues, coastal recreation and mild winters; nightlife is pleasant but not Erasmus-scale. Living costs are low and the country has an established Jewish community.

Good technical university with lively student nightlife but campuses are city-integrated rather than a single residential bubble—less ideal for the unified-campus preference. Turin has strong museums and historic architecture with cooler yet not extreme winters; Jewish community is present and accessible.

Excellent cultural match for museums, history and nightlife, but Berlin is a sprawling, commuter-style city with scattered campuses—poor fit if you want a unified, residential campus. Strong international community and vibrant Jewish/Israeli presence, and costs are moderate for Germany.

    - `lifestyle_fit`: Score the combined physical routine and social atmosphere. Evaluate the physical routine based on Campus Typology (enclosed residential bubble vs. 
        decentralized commuter school), City Scale (immersive college town vs. sprawling megacity), and Academic Pacing (hyper-competitive "pressure-cooker" vs. balanced workload).

        STRICTLY IGNORE general city crime rates, pickpocketing, or broad safety metrics.
    - `other_preferences_fit`: Any specific user requests that do not fit into the above categories (e.g., specific sports, dietary needs, unique hobbies).

academic.instruction_languages: Most courses are in German; a number of courses are available in English (mainly at graduate level).
academic.academic_summary_notes: Exchange students must meet language requirements (German or English) to apply; they pay tuition at home but must cover a student social fund contribution (~€80). A preparatory German intensive course (early Sep/Mar) costs approx. €295 and awards 6 ECTS; Erasmus students must have completed A2 to be eligible for the preparatory course.

housing_and_logistics.housing_details: Dorm rooms via studierendenWERK Berlin (rent €350-€400) can be applied for after exchange application deadlines; housing is not guaranteed. Students advised to arrive ~2 weeks before orientation to find private accommodation if necessary. More info: https://www.tu.berlin/en/go41781/
housing_and_logistics.medical_and_insurance_details: Health insurance if not waived approx. €100/month; students applying for visa/residence permit must prove sufficient financial resources (see below).
housing_and_logistics.estimated_housing_cost_per_month: Dorm: €350-€400/month; general housing estimate €350-€650/month depending on type and location.
housing_and_logistics.estimated_living_cost_per_month: Housing €350-650 / food €150 / books & supplies €40 / health insurance (if not waived) €100; public transport approx. €180 per semester. Students applying for a visa/residence permit must demonstrate ~€934/month.
housing_and_logistics.logistics_summary_notes: Students needing a visa must prove sufficient funds (~€934/month). Housing via university is limited and not guaranteed; apply when instructed after exchange deadlines. Insurance is required unless waived and estimated at ~€100/month.

student_integration.language_course_details: Preparatory German intensive course offered early September/early March for approx. €295 (6 ECTS). Erasmus students eligible only with completed A2 German. German courses also available during the semester via ZEMS.
student_integration.integration_summary_notes: TU Berlin offers a preparatory German course and orientation sessions for exchange students and runs a buddy program to support integration.

academic.grading_system_summary: Local numeric scale 0-20 (French system); pass >=10 with subgroups A (outstanding) to E; FX/F for failures. ECTS maps passing students to A (top 10%), B (next 25%), C (next 30%), D (next 25%), E (last 10%); failures split into FX (local >=7) and F (local <7).
academic.academic_summary_notes: Courses are mainly taught in French (recommended CEFR level B1). Exchange students apply via the online portal and must meet nomination deadlines (1 Dec for autumn, 1 May for spring).

housing_and_logistics.housing_details: The institution provides guidance and assistance in finding accommodation and lists platforms such as HousingAnywhere and ESN; contact Incoming Relations Officer (incoming@centrale-marseille.fr) and international student webpages for support.
housing_and_logistics.medical_and_insurance_details: The institution assists incoming students/staff in obtaining insurance and will inform cases where cover is not automatically provided; contact incoming@centrale-marseille.fr and the international student webpages for details. No costs specified.
housing_and_logistics.logistics_summary_notes: The university assists with visa procedures and housing searches and provides insurance assistance; nomination deadlines are 1 Dec (autumn) and 1 May (spring), decisions sent within ~4 weeks and transcripts within ~5 weeks.

student_integration.integration_summary_notes: The International Students' Association (ICM) offers information and guidance to incoming students; institutional contacts (incoming@centrale-marseille.fr) and partner platforms (ESN) support integration and accommodation.
